final.title: Early signs your AI workflow is drifting
final.body:
Eval drift is not a theory problem for a small business. It is a workflow problem. If an AI-assisted process starts giving answers that are inconsistent, off-target, or a little too confident for comfort, the question is not whether the model has become sentient. It is whether the workflow still deserves to stay on autopilot.

The practical check is simple: do you already have one recurring, high-frequency task where AI filters, ranks, or responds to inputs, and would drift show up as customer complaints, missed approvals, failed orders, or manual rework? If not, there is nothing to monitor yet. If yes, write down one control.

A sensible first control is a monthly manual spot-check against a small sample of past cases using the original success criteria. Keep it human-readable: what came in, what the system output, and whether a person would still sign off on it. Any threshold you use should be your own operating rule, not a Bareni benchmark.

In a free 30-minute diagnostic, the question is simply whether eval drift is a real risk in this workflow, and whether the workflow is live. If it is, we can decide whether drift monitoring belongs in the pilot scope or whether it is still too early to tackle. Human approval stays in place before any retraining or policy change. For a small business, that is usually the part worth keeping boring.

final.title: Early signs your AI workflow is drifting
final.body:
Eval drift is not a theory problem for a small business; it is a workflow problem. If an AI-assisted process starts giving answers that are inconsistent, off-target, or too confident for the evidence in front of it, the question is not whether the model has become sentient. It is whether the workflow still deserves to stay on autopilot.

The practical check is simple: do you already have one repetitive, high-frequency task where AI filters, ranks, or responds to inputs, and would drift show up as customer complaints, missed approvals, failed orders, or manual rework? If not, there is nothing to monitor yet. If yes, pick one control and write it down.

A sensible first control is a monthly manual spot-check against a small set of past cases using the original success criteria. Keep it human-readable: what came in, what the system output, and whether a person would still sign off on it. Any threshold you use should be your own operating rule, not a benchmark borrowed from elsewhere.

In a free 30-minute diagnostic, the useful question is: “Is eval drift a real risk in this workflow, or are we trying to solve a problem we do not have yet?” That keeps the decision bounded. If drift monitoring belongs anywhere, it belongs inside a pilot scope with human approval before any retraining or policy change. That is the kind of decision a pilot should test before anyone treats the workflow as stable.
